facts.statement: Brachiosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian to Tithonian),

facts.statement: The genus Brachiosaurus was first described by Elmer S. Riggs in 1903.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Riggs (1903)

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Brachiosaurus altithorax.
facts.quote: species: altithorax

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus was first described from fossils found in the Colorado River valley in western Colorado, United States.
facts.quote: It was first described by American paleontologist Elmer S. Riggs in 1903 from fossils found in the Colorado River valley in western Colorado, United States.

facts.statement: The generic name Brachiosaurus means "arm lizard" and the specific name altithorax means "deep chest".
facts.quote: Riggs named the dinosaur Brachiosaurus altithorax; the generic name is Greek for "arm lizard", in reference to its proportionately long arms, and the specific name means "deep chest".

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus is estimated to have been between 18 and 22 meters long, with a body mass ranging from 28.3 to 46.9 metric tons for the subadult holotype.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus is estimated to have been between 18 and 22 m long; body mass estimates of the subadult holotype specimen range from 28.3 to 46.9 MT.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus had a disproportionately long neck, a small skull, and a large overall size.
facts.quote: It had a disproportionately long neck, small skull, and large overall size, all of which are typical for sauropods.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus is the namesake genus of the family Brachiosauridae.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus is the namesake genus of the family Brachiosauridae, which includes a handful of other similar sauropods.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus is regarded as a high browser that could reach vegetation up to 9 meters off the ground.
facts.quote: It is regarded as a high browser, possibly cropping or nipping vegetation as high as 9 m off the ground.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus was unsuited for rearing on its hindlimbs, unlike other sauropods.
facts.quote: Unlike other sauropods, it was unsuited for rearing on its hindlimbs.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Brachiosaurus was ectothermic or warm-blooded, with recent research suggesting it was warm-blooded.
facts.quote: It has been used as an example of a dinosaur that was most likely ectothermic because of its large size and the corresponding need for sufficient forage, but more recent research suggests it was warm-blooded.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen comes from the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation and dates to about 154 to 153 million years ago.
facts.quote: This specimen, which was later declared the holotype, comes from rocks of the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation, and therefore is late Kimmeridgian in age, about 154to 153million years old.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen is cataloged as FMNHP25107 and was discovered by Elmer S. Riggs and his crew from the Field Columbian Museum.
facts.quote: Discovered by American paleontologist Elmer S. Riggs and his crew from the Field Columbian Museum (now the Field Museum of Natural History) of Chicago, it is currently cataloged as FMNHP25107.

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton includes the right humerus, femur, ilium, coracoid, sacrum, seven thoracic vertebrae, two caudal vertebrae, and several ribs.
facts.quote: The holotype skeleton consists of the right humerus (upper arm bone), the right femur (thigh bone), the right ilium (a hip bone), the right coracoid (a shoulder bone), the sacrum (fused vertebrae of the hip), the last seven thoracic (trunk) and two caudal (tail) vertebrae, and several ribs.

facts.statement: Restudy has shown that the coracoid in the holotype is from the right side of the body, contrary to Riggs's original description.
facts.quote: Riggs described the coracoid as from the left side of the body, but restudy has shown it to be a right coracoid.

facts.statement: In 1901, Elmer Riggs published a report on a new dinosaur find, noting its unusual arm length relative to its leg length and its extreme overall size.
facts.quote: Riggs published a short report of the new find in 1901, noting the unusual length of the humerus compared to the femur and the extreme overall size and the resulting giraffe-like proportions

facts.statement: Elmer Riggs named the type species Brachiosaurus altithorax in 1903.
facts.quote: In 1903, he named the type species Brachiosaurus altithorax.

facts.statement: Riggs derived the genus name Brachiosaurus from Greek words for "arm" and "lizard" because the specimen had unusually long arms for a sauropod.
facts.quote: Riggs derived the genus name from the Greek brachion/βραχίων meaning "arm" and sauros/σαυρος meaning "lizard", because he realized that the length of the arms was unusual for a sauropod.

facts.statement: The specific epithet altithorax was chosen to describe the specimen's unusually deep and wide chest cavity.
facts.quote: The specific epithet was chosen because of the unusually deep and wide chest cavity, from Latin altus "deep" and Greek thorax/θώραξ, "breastplate, cuirass, corslet".

facts.statement: Elmer Riggs published a detailed monograph describing the specimen in 1904.
facts.quote: Riggs followed his 1903 publication with a more detailed description in a monograph in 1904.

facts.statement: Preparation of the Brachiosaurus holotype began in the fall of 1900 after it was collected by Elmer Riggs for the Field Museum.
facts.quote: Preparation of the holotype began in the fall of 1900 shortly after it was collected by Riggs for the Field Museum.

facts.statement: James B. Abbott and C.T. Kline prepared the weathered back and hip vertebrae of the holotype in the winter of 1904.
facts.quote: In the winter of 1904, the badly weathered vertebrae of the back and hip were prepared by James B. Abbott and C.T. Kline.

facts.statement: By 1908, the individual bones of the holotype were displayed separately in Hall 35 of the Field Museum.
facts.quote: All the bones were, solitarily, still on display by 1908 in Hall 35 when the Field Museum's newly mounted Apatosaurus was unveiled

facts.statement: In 1993, the holotype bones were cast and missing parts were sculpted using material from the related species Brachiosaurus brancai.
facts.quote: In 1993, the holotype bones were molded and cast, and the missing bones were sculpted based on material of the related Brachiosaurus brancai (now Giraffatitan) in Museum für Naturkunde, Berlin.

facts.statement: The reconstructed plastic skeleton of the holotype was mounted and displayed in Stanley Field Hall in 1994.
facts.quote: This plastic skeleton was mounted and, in 1994, put on display at the north end of Stanley Field Hall, the main exhibit hall of the Field Museum's current building.

facts.statement: The original mount was moved to O'Hare International Airport in 1999 to make space for the Tyrannosaurus skeleton "Sue".
facts.quote: The mount stood until 1999, when it was moved to the BConcourse of United Airlines' Terminal One in O'Hare International Airport to make room for the museum's newly acquired Tyrannosaurus skeleton, "Sue".

facts.statement: A second outdoor cast of the skeleton was displayed on the museum's terrace until 2022.
facts.quote: At the same time, the Field Museum mounted a second plastic cast of the skeleton (designed for outside use) which was on display outside the museum on the NW terrace until 2022.

facts.statement: An outdoor cast was installed at Disney's Animal Kingdom as a gateway icon for the "DinoLand, U.S.A." area.
facts.quote: Another outdoor cast was sent to Disney's Animal Kingdom to serve as a gateway icon for the "DinoLand, U.S.A." area, known as the "Oldengate Bridge" that connects the two halves of the fossil quarry themed Boneyard play area.

facts.statement: Additional discoveries of Brachiosaurus material in North America are uncommon and consist of only a few bones.
facts.quote: Further discoveries of Brachiosaurus material in North America have been uncommon and consist of a few bones.

facts.statement: In 1883, Marshall Parker Felch reported finding a sauropod skull in Felch Quarry 1 near Garden Park, Colorado.
facts.quote: In 1883, farmer Marshall Parker Felch, a fossil collector for the American paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh, reported the discovery of a sauropod skull in Felch Quarry 1, near Garden Park, Colorado.

facts.statement: In 1998, Carpenter and Tidwell formally assigned the Felch Quarry skull to Brachiosaurus sp. because it could not be determined if it belonged to B. altithorax.
facts.quote: In 1998 Carpenter and Tidwell described the Felch Quarry skull, and formally assigned it to Brachiosaurus sp. (of uncertain species), since it is impossible to determine whether it belonged to the species B. altithorax itself

facts.statement: In 2019, Michael D. D'Emic and Matthew T. Carrano re-examined the Felch Quarry skull using preparation and CT scanning.
facts.quote: In 2019, American paleontologists Michael D. D'Emic and Matthew T. Carrano re-examined the Felch Quarry skull after having it further prepared and CT-scanned

facts.statement: A shoulder blade and coracoid from Dry Mesa Quarry, Colorado, were central to the debate over Supersaurus and Ultrasauros in the 1980s and 1990s.
facts.quote: A shoulder blade with coracoid from Dry Mesa Quarry, Colorado, is one of the specimens at the center of the Supersaurus/Ultrasauros issue of the 1980s and 1990s.

facts.statement: In 1996, Brian Curtice and colleagues assigned the Dry Mesa shoulder blade (specimen BYU 9462) to Brachiosaurus sp.
facts.quote: The shoulder blade, specimen BYU 9462 (previously BYU 5001), was in 1996 assigned to a Brachiosaurus sp. (of uncertain species) by Brian Curtice and colleagues

facts.statement: In 2009, Michael P. Taylor concluded that the Dry Mesa shoulder blade could not be referred to B. altithorax.
facts.quote: in 2009 Michael P. Taylor concluded that it could not be referred to B. altithorax.

facts.statement: The animal represented by the Dry Mesa shoulder blade was smaller than Riggs's original Brachiosaurus specimen.
facts.quote: The Dry Mesa "ultrasaur" was not as large as had been thought; the dimensions of the shoulder's coracoid bone indicate that the animal was smaller than Riggs's original specimen of Brachiosaurus.

facts.statement: A humerus belonging to a potential Brachiosaurus specimen was discovered in 1943 by uranium prospectors in western Colorado.
facts.quote: One of these finds, the humerus USNM 21903, was discovered in ca. 1943 by uranium prospectors Vivian and Daniel Jones in the Potter Creek Quarry in western Colorado, and donated to the Smithsonian Institution.

facts.statement: A nearly complete juvenile skeleton approximately 2 meters long was reported in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2012, José Carballido and colleagues reported a nearly complete postcranial skeleton of a small juvenile approximately 2 m in length.

facts.statement: A juvenile Brachiosaurus specimen nicknamed "Toni" was found in the Morrison Formation of north-central Wyoming.
facts.quote: This specimen, nicknamed "Toni" and cataloged as SMA 0009, stems from the Morrison Formation of the Bighorn Basin in north-central Wyoming.

facts.statement: In 2019, researchers questioned the classification of two specific Brachiosaurus specimens into their respective clades.
facts.quote: However, the assignment of these two specimens to their respective clades was later questioned by D'Emic and Carrano in 2019.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that the assignment of the juvenile specimen "Toni" to B. altithorax might be based on mistaken interpretations.
facts.quote: They considered the referral of "Toni" to B. altithorax be based on mistaken interpretations of the species' unique features or of the specimen itself, and deemed it worthy of further study.

facts.statement: Between 1909 and 1912, expeditions in German East Africa uncovered significant brachiosaurid fossils from the Tendaguru Formation.
facts.quote: Between 1909 and 1912, large-scale paleontological expeditions in German East Africa unearthed a considerable amount of brachiosaurid material from the Tendaguru Formation.

facts.statement: In 1914, Werner Janensch concluded that fossils from the Tendaguru Formation belonged to the genus Brachiosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1914, German paleontologist Werner Janensch listed differences and commonalities between these fossils and B. altithorax, concluding they could be referred to the genus Brachiosaurus.

facts.statement: Werner Janensch named two species from the Tendaguru material: Brachiosaurus brancai and Brachiosaurus fraasi.
facts.quote: From this material Janensch named two species: Brachiosaurus brancai for the larger and more complete taxon, and Brachiosaurus fraasi for the smaller and more poorly known species.

facts.statement: A nearly complete skeleton was collected in 1930 by F.W.H. Migeod for the British Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: Additional material was collected by the British Museum of Natural History's Tendaguru expedition, including a nearly complete skeleton (BMNH R5937) collected by F.W.H. Migeod in 1930.

facts.statement: The description of Brachiosaurus brancai was based on "Skelett S," which was later found to consist of two partial individuals.
facts.quote: Janensch based his description of B. brancai on "Skelett S" (skeleton S) from Tendaguru, but later realized that it comprised two partial individuals: SI and SII.

facts.statement: In 1935, Janensch designated skeleton SI as the lectotype for Brachiosaurus brancai.
facts.quote: He at first did not designate them as a syntype series, but in 1935 made SI (presently MB.R.2180) the lectotype.

facts.statement: In 2009, Taylor proposed skeleton SII as the lectotype, unaware that Janensch had already designated SI.
facts.quote: Taylor in 2009, unaware of this action, proposed the larger and more complete SII (MB.R.2181) as the lectotype.

facts.statement: While Daniel Chure rejected the split in 2010, most studies from 2012 onward accepted the name Giraffatitan.
facts.quote: The split was rejected by Daniel Chure in 2010, but from 2012 onward most studies recognized the name Giraffatitan.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurid remains were discovered in 1947 at Atalaia, Portugal, in Tithonian layers.
facts.quote: In 1947, at Atalaia in Portugal, brachiosaurid remains were found in layers dating from the Tithonian.

facts.statement: Albert-Félix de Lapparent and Georges Zbyszewski named the Portuguese remains Brachiosaurus atalaiensis in 1957.
facts.quote: Albert-Félix de Lapparent and Georges Zbyszewski named them as the species Brachiosaurus atalaiensis in 1957.

facts.statement: In 2004, Upchurch, Barrett, and Dodson doubted the referral of the Portuguese species to Brachiosaurus.
facts.quote: Its referral to Brachiosaurus was doubted in the 2004 edition of The Dinosauria by Paul Upchurch, Barret, and Peter Dodson who listed it as an as yet unnamed brachiosaurid genus.

facts.statement: In 2003, Antunes and Mateus placed the Portuguese species in its own genus, Lusotitan.
facts.quote: Shortly before the publication of the 2004 book, the species had been placed in its own genus Lusotitan by Miguel Telles Antunes and Octávio Mateus in 2003.

facts.statement: An analysis in 2013 confirmed that Lusotitan is a brachiosaurid based on specific skeletal features.
facts.quote: The low neural spines, the prominent deltopectoral crest of the humerus (a muscle attachment site on the upper arm bone), the elongated humerus (very long and slender), and the long axis of the ilium tilting upward indicate that Lusotitan is a brachiosaurid, which was confirmed by some later studies, such as an analysis in 2013.

facts.statement: Fragmentary brachiosaurid remains were reported in eastern Algeria in 1958 by French petroleum geologist F. Nougarède.
facts.quote: In 1958 French petroleum geologist F. Nougarède reported to have discovered fragmentary brachiosaurid remains in eastern Algeria, in the Sahara Desert.

facts.statement: Albert-Félix de Lapparent described and named the species Brachiosaurus nougaredi in 1960 based on the Algerian remains.
facts.quote: Based on these, Albert-Félix de Lapparent described and named the species Brachiosaurus nougaredi in 1960.

facts.statement: The type material of B. nougaredi consists of a sacrum and some left metacarpals and phalanges found in eastern Algeria.
facts.quote: The type material moved to Paris consisted of a sacrum, weathered out at the desert surface, and some of the left metacarpals and phalanges.

facts.statement: A 2013 analysis suggested that the remains of B. nougaredi possibly belong to more than one species because they were collected far apart.
facts.quote: B. nougaredi was in 2004 considered to represent a distinct, unnamed brachiosaurid genus, but a 2013 analysis by Philip D. Mannion and colleagues found that the remains possibly belong to more than one species, as they were collected far apart.

facts.statement: The metacarpals found in Algeria were concluded to belong to an indeterminate titanosauriform.
facts.quote: The metacarpals were concluded to belong to some indeterminate titanosauriform.

facts.statement: The genus Brachiosaurus was established by Elmer S. Riggs in 1903.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Riggs, 1903

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 154 to 153 million years ago, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió durante el Jurásico Superior, hace aproximadamente 154 a 153 millones de años, en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus was first described by Elmer S. Riggs in 1903 from fossils found in the Grand Canyon area of Colorado, USA.
facts.quote: Fue descrita por primera vez por Elmer S. Riggs en 1903 a partir de fósiles encontrados en el río del Gran Cañón, ahora Río Colorado del oeste de Colorado, en sedimentos de la famosa Formación Morrison, Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus had an extremely long neck, a small skull, and a large overall size, which are typical traits of sauropods.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus tiene el cuello extremadamente largo, un cráneo pequeño y gran tamaño general, todos los cuales son rasgos típicos de los saurópodos.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus had front legs longer than its hind legs and a relatively shorter tail compared to its neck, distinguishing it from most other Jurassic sauropods.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus tiene proporciones que son diferentes de la mayoría de los saurópodos, siendo las patas delanteras más largas que las patas traseras, característica a la que hace referencia su nombre, y su cola era más corta en proporción a su cuello que otros saurópodos del Jurásico.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus was likely a high browser that fed on vegetation up to 9 meters above the ground.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus es considerado como un alto ramoneador, que probablemente hubiese mordisqueado o pellizcado la vegetación de la copa de los árboles posiblemente tan alto como 9 metros por encima del suelo.

facts.statement: Recent research indicates that Brachiosaurus was likely endothermic (warm-blooded), contrary to earlier hypotheses based on its size.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus se ha utilizado como un ejemplo de un dinosaurio que era probablemente ectotérmico debido a su gran tamaño y su necesidad de alimentación, pero investigaciones más recientes han demostrado que habría sido de sangre caliente.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus was a quadrupedal sauropod with a small skull, long neck, relatively short muscular tail, and columnar limbs.
facts.quote: Al igual que todos los dinosaurios saurópodos, Brachiosaurus era un animal cuadrúpedo con un cráneo pequeño, cuello largo, una cola relativamente corta, musculosa y delgada, extremidades columnares.

facts.statement: The humerus of the type specimen of Brachiosaurus measures 2.04 meters in length and is relatively light for its size.
facts.quote: El húmero,hueso del brazo, de Brachiosaurus es relativamente ligero por su tamaño, que mide 2,04 metros de longitud en el espécimen tipo.

facts.statement: The femur of the type specimen of Brachiosaurus measures only 2.03 meters in length.
facts.quote: El fémur, hueso del muslo, del espécimen tipo mide solamente 2,03 metros de largo.

facts.statement: Unlike other sauropods, Brachiosaurus had a slightly slanted shoulder joint and an unusually deep rib cage.
facts.quote: A diferencia de otros saurópodos, Brachiosaurus parece haber tenido ligeramente tumbada la articulación del hombro, y la caja torácica era inusualmente profunda.

facts.statement: The deep rib cage caused Brachiosaurus's trunk to be inclined, with the front much higher than the hips and the neck emerging at a sharp angle.
facts.quote: Esto hacía que el tronco estuviese inclinado, con la parte delantera mucho más alta que las caderas, además el cuello sale del tronco en un ángulo pronunciado.

facts.statement: Most size estimates for Brachiosaurus are actually based on the African species Giraffatitan brancai because more complete material is known for it.
facts.quote: Debido a que se conoce material mucho más completo de Giraffatitan "Brachiosaurus" brancai que de B. altithorax, la mayoría de las estimaciones del tamaño de Brachiosaurus son en realidad de la forma africana.

facts.statement: Estimates for the mass of B. altithorax have varied over time, ranging from 28.7 to 56.3 metric tons in recent studies.
facts.quote: Con los años, la masa de B. altithorax se ha estimado en 35,0 toneladas por Paul en 1988, 43,9 toneladas por Foster en 2003, 28,7 toneladas por Taylor en 2009 y, más recientemente, en 56,3 toneladas métricas por Benson en 2014.

facts.statement: The length of Brachiosaurus has been estimated at 26 meters.
facts.quote: La longitud del Brachiosaurus se ha estimado en 26 metros.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurids had a back sloping toward the tail due to their long front legs, unlike most other sauropods.
facts.quote: En contraste con la mayoría de otros saurópodos, los braquiosáuridos tenían la espalda inclinada hacia la zona caudal, debido a sus largas patas delanteras.

facts.statement: Walter Janensch described the Tendaguru sauropod material in 1914, listing differences and similarities with Brachiosaurus altithorax.
facts.quote: Al describir el material del braquiosáurido de Tendaguru en 1914, Janensch enumeró una serie de diferencias y similitudes entre ellos y B. altithorax.

facts.statement: Gregory Paul published a new skeletal reconstruction of "B." brancai in 1988, highlighting proportional differences between it and B. altithorax.
facts.quote: En 1988, Gregory Paul publicó una nueva reconstrucción del esqueleto de "B." brancai, destacando una serie de diferencias en proporción entre este y B. altithorax.

facts.statement: Michael Taylor found significant differences between B. altithorax and the Tendaguru material in 2009 across all known skeletal elements.
facts.quote: Un estudio detallado de todo el material, incluyendo los huesos de la extremidad y de la cintura, por Michael Taylor en 2009 encontró que hay diferencias significativas entre B. altithorax y el material de Tendaguru en todos los elementos conocidos de ambas especies.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus is the eponymous genus of the family Brachiosauridae.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus es el género epónimo de Brachiosauridae, familia a la que le da nombre.

facts.statement: Many sauropods, including Astrodon, Bothriospondylus, Dinodocus, Pelorosaurus, Pleurocoelus, and Ultrasaurus, have been assigned to Brachiosauridae but are now considered doubtful or of uncertain placement.
facts.quote: A través de los años, una serie de saurópodos han sido asignados a Brachiosauridae, como Astrodon, Bothriospondylus, Dinodocus, Pelorosaurus, Pleurocoelus, y Ultrasaurus, pero la mayoría de ellos se consideran actualmente como dudosos o de colocación incierta.

facts.statement: According to Taylor's revised diagnosis, Brachiosaurus altithorax is characterized by many distinctive traits, many of which are found on the posterior dorsal vertebrae.
facts.quote: De acuerdo con el diagnóstico revisado por Taylor, Brachiosaurus altithorax se diagnostica como una plétora de rasgos distintivos muchos de los cuales se encuentran en la parte posterior de las vértebras dorsales.

facts.statement: Traits placing Brachiosaurus in Brachiosauridae include a humerus to femur length ratio of at least 0.9 and a very flattened femoral shaft (ratio ≥1.85).
facts.quote: Entre los rasgos distintivos que lo colocan en la familia Brachiosauridae son una relación entre la longitud del húmero al fémur longitud de al menos 0,9 (es decir, el hueso del brazo superior es al menos casi tan largo como el hueso del muslo), y un eje del fémur es muy aplanada (relación ≥1.85).

facts.statement: The family Brachiosauridae is located at the base of Titanosauriformes, a sauropod group that also includes titanosaurs.
facts.quote: Brachiosauridae está situada en la base de Titanosauriformes, un grupo de saurópodos, que también incluye a los titanosaurios.

facts.statement: A cladogram of Brachiosauridae was published by D'Emic in 2012.
facts.quote: Cladograma de Brachiosauridae después de D'Emic (2012).

facts.statement: The genus Brachiosaurus was named by Elmer S. Riggs in 1903.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Brachiosaurus (genus), Riggs 1903

facts.statement: The parent group of the genus Brachiosaurus is the family Brachiosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Brachiosauridae

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus belongs to the class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Brachiosaurus is Brachiosaurus altithorax.
facts.quote: Type species: Brachiosaurus altithorax

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus altithorax is distinguished from African material by uniform trunk vertebrae, whereas the African material shows wide variation.
facts.quote: La principal es una diferencia en la forma en que varían las vértebras del tronco, son bastante uniformes en B. altithorax, pero varían ampliamente en el material africano.

rejected.statement: Brachiosaurus had longer forelimbs than hindlimbs, resulting in a steeply inclined trunk and a proportionally shorter tail.
rejected.quote: Atypically, Brachiosaurus had longer forelimbs than hindlimbs, which resulted in a steeply inclined trunk and a proportionally shorter tail.

rejected.quote: During a prospecting trip on horseback, Riggs's field assistant Harold William Menke found the humerus of FMNHP25107, on July 4, exclaiming it was "the biggest thing yet!".

rejected.statement: Riggs suggested in 1904 that the missing front part of the holotype was washed away by a water current while the hind part was preserved under sediment.
rejected.quote: Based on this evidence, Riggs in 1904 suggested that the missing front part of the skeleton was washed away by a water current, while the hind part was already covered by sediment and thus got preserved.

rejected.statement: D'Emic and Carrano concluded in 2019 that the skull most likely belongs to B. altithorax because no other brachiosaurid taxa are known from the Morrison Formation.
rejected.quote: They also found it most parsimonious to assign the skull to B. altithorax itself rather than an unspecified species, as there is no evidence of other brachiosaurid taxa in the Morrison Formation

rejected.statement: The largest sauropod foot ever found was reported in 2018 from the Black Hills of Weston County, Wyoming.
rejected.quote: In 2018, the largest sauropod foot ever found was reported from the Black Hills of Weston County, Wyoming.

rejected.statement: Gregory S. Paul suggested in 1988 that the African and North American species should be separated only at the subgenus level.
rejected.quote: Paul believed that the limb and girdle elements of both species were very similar, and therefore suggested they be separated not at genus, but only at subgenus level, as Brachiosaurus (Brachiosaurus) altithorax and Brachiosaurus (Giraffatitan) brancai.

rejected.statement: A 2009 study by Taylor argued that the African material should be classified as the separate genus Giraffatitan based on twenty-six distinct bone characters.
rejected.quote: Taylor found twenty-six distinct osteological (bone-based) characters, a larger difference than between Diplodocus and Barosaurus, and therefore argued that the African material should indeed be placed in its own genus (Giraffatitan) as Giraffatitan brancai.

rejected.statement: Michael Taylor argued in 2009 that the African material should be placed in its own genus, Giraffatitan, based on 26 distinct osteological characters.
rejected.quote: Taylor encontró 26 caracteres osteológicos distintos, una diferencia mayor que la existente entre, por ejemplo, Diplodocus y Barosaurus, y por lo tanto argumentó que el material africano debería ser colocado en su propio género, Giraffatitan, con la especie G. brancai.
